```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 100

```

Every spax model needs three inputs that line up: demand (the people who may
use a service, counted where they live), supply (what each facility offers)
and the travel time between them. This guide answers one question: how do I
get my own data into that shape? It prepares the inputs with `prep_data()` and
works through three problems you are likely to meet: facility IDs that must
match, travel times that are unknown, and demand that comes as area totals
rather than a grid. It ends with the inputs of the allocation model, including
observed counts in a long table. The examples use the Cornwall GP data,
described in [The Cornwall GP example data](cornwall-data.html). The `spax()`
interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later
versions.

The guide uses spax with terra for the grids, sf for the small areas and dplyr
for tables.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

## The inputs

`prep_data()` takes two shapes of input. The first sections use rasters: a
demand grid, a stack of travel layers and a table of facilities, as for the
FCA indices. The last two use vectors and a travel matrix named by ID, as for
the allocation model. The code reads the population grid, the stack of travel
times and the table of all practices, the Isles of Scilly included.

```{r data}
# Residents per grid cell (WorldPop 2020)
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
# Travel minutes, one layer per practice
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
# Practices as a plain table
gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)

c(practices = nrow(gp), travel_layers = nlyr(travel_grid))
head(names(travel_grid))
```

Each travel layer is named with the practice's NHS code, the same code as in
`gp$practice`. That shared code is what lines the inputs up.

## Match facilities by ID, not by order

`prep_data()` takes the table of practices with two more arguments: `id_col`
names the column of facility IDs and `supply_cols` the column of supply. spax
then matches each row of the table to the travel layer with the same ID. To
see this, the code computes an accessibility index from the table in its own
order and in reverse order. The index is an enhanced two-step floating
catchment area index (E2SFCA, one of the FCA indices): GP full-time
equivalents (FTE) per resident, with nearer practices counting more. Its weights
fall with travel time on a
Gaussian curve, and the travel scale σ, which sets how fast they fall, is 10
minutes, as in [Getting started](spax.html).

```{r id-order}
e2sfca <- spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10))

# The practices in their own order, and in reverse order
in_order <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
reversed <- prep_data(pop, arrange(gp, desc(practice)), travel_grid,
                      id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

index_in_order <- spax(in_order, e2sfca)
index_reversed <- spax(reversed, e2sfca)
all.equal(values(index_in_order$accessibility), values(index_reversed$accessibility))
```

`spax()` returns the index as a raster in the result's `accessibility`
element, in GP FTE per resident. The two indices are equal: the row order of the
table does not matter. A
named supply vector is matched by name in the same way. An unnamed vector or a
matrix is used in layer order, and then keeping the order right is your job.

A facility that is in one input and not the other stops with an error. Here
the table drops the Scilly practice while the travel stack keeps its layer:

```{r id-missing, error = TRUE}
prep_data(pop, filter(gp, !scilly), travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
```

The error compares counts: `r nlyr(travel_grid)` travel layers against
`r sum(!gp$scilly)` practices. To keep only some facilities, select their
layers by ID, `travel_grid[[ids]]`, as the grid recipe in the next section
does with `[[gp$practice]]`. A code in the table that matches no layer, such as
a typing error, passes
`prep_data()` but stops with an error when `spax()` runs the model.

## Decide what unknown travel means

For an FCA index, an unknown (`NA`) travel time means no access: the pair is
left out of the sums. Decide whether that is true for your gaps before you
compute an index. In the Cornwall travel grid, `NA` marks cells with no
residents, pairs with no road connection and journeys over 180 minutes. Here
the gaps come from the Isles of Scilly: their practice cannot be reached by
road from the mainland, mainland practices cannot be reached from the islands,
and some cells on the smaller islands reach no practice at all. The code
counts the populated cells with unknown travel in each practice's layer, then
the residents of the cells with a road route to each side.

```{r travel-na}
# Count the populated cells with unknown travel in each practice's layer
populated <- !is.na(pop)
missing_cells <- global(is.na(travel_grid) & populated, "sum")[[1]]
table(scilly_practice = gp$scilly, missing_cells)

# Cells with a road route to the Scilly practice (L82017) or to the
# mainland (here the first layer, a mainland practice)
road_scilly <- !is.na(values(travel_grid[["L82017"]], mat = FALSE))
road_mainland <- !is.na(values(travel_grid[[1]], mat = FALSE))

# Residents in each group
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
by_route <- round(c(
  to_mainland = sum(residents[road_mainland]),
  to_scilly_practice = sum(residents[road_scilly]),
  no_road_link = sum(residents[!road_mainland & !road_scilly], na.rm = TRUE)
))
by_route
```

Each mainland layer has `r min(missing_cells)` populated cells with unknown
travel, all on the islands, and the Scilly layer has
`r format(max(missing_cells), big.mark = ",")`, every mainland cell among
them. Of the residents,
`r format(by_route[["to_mainland"]], big.mark = ",")` live in cells with a
road route to the mainland practices,
`r format(by_route[["to_scilly_practice"]], big.mark = ",")` in cells that
reach the Scilly practice and `r by_route[["no_road_link"]]` in cells that
reach neither.

The index above used all `r nrow(gp)` practices. The code compares its median
in the two groups of cells, per 1,000 residents.

```{r scilly-effect}
# Index per 1,000 residents with all practices
with_scilly <- 1000 * values(index_in_order$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
scilly_medians <- round(c(
  mainland_median = median(with_scilly[road_mainland]),
  scilly_median = median(with_scilly[road_scilly])
), 2)
scilly_medians
```

The islands become a separate system with one practice and few residents, so
their median index is `r scilly_medians[["scilly_median"]]` GP FTE per 1,000
residents against `r scilly_medians[["mainland_median"]]` on the mainland. The
cells that reach no practice get no index (`NA`), and their residents drop out
of every practice's demand.

The islands do have access, by boat and air, which the road-based travel times
do not represent. So the guides model mainland Cornwall only, with the grid
recipe from [The Cornwall GP example data](cornwall-data.html). The last line
looks for populated cells with an unknown travel time.

```{r mainland}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

# Any populated cell with an unknown travel time?
anyNA(values(travel_grid)[!is.na(values(pop)), ])
```

`FALSE`: every populated cell of the mainland grid has a travel time to every
mainland practice. [The Cornwall GP example
data](cornwall-data.html#a-grid-for-the-fca-indices) explains each line of the
recipe. For the allocation model, `prep_data()` asks you to choose what
unknown travel means, as [Inputs for the allocation
model](#inputs-for-the-allocation-model) shows below.

## Turn area totals into a demand grid

Demand often comes as totals for administrative areas, while an index on a
grid needs a count of people per cell. `cornwall_lsoa` holds ONS
mid-2024 population estimates for `r sum(!cornwall_lsoa$scilly)` mainland
small areas (LSOAs). Spreading each total evenly over its cells would ignore
where people live inside the area, so the WorldPop grid serves as a pattern:
`transform_pmf()` turns it into shares that sum to 1, and `transform_demand()`
rescales those shares so that each area keeps its own total. The code spreads
the totals of the small areas.

```{r lsoa-too-small}
# Mainland small areas as a terra vector in the grid's coordinates
lsoa <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_transform(crs(pop)) |>
  vect()

# The WorldPop grid as shares that sum to 1
pattern <- transform_pmf(pop)

# Spread each area's total over its cells
# (density = TRUE returns people per cell; FALSE returns shares)
lsoa_grid <- transform_demand(x = lsoa, value_col = "pop", pmf = pattern, density = TRUE)
```

The grid cells are about 1 km across, and many town LSOAs are smaller. An area
whose polygon contains no cell center cannot receive its count. The function
drops those areas and rescales the grid to the overall total, so their
residents would land in other areas' cells. The fix is larger areas or a finer
grid. Here the code merges the LSOAs into their middle-layer areas (MSOAs): an
LSOA name ends in a letter, and dropping it gives the MSOA name (Cornwall 013A
is in Cornwall 013).

```{r msoa}
# Merge LSOAs into MSOAs, adding up their counts
# (terra names the summed columns sum_pop, sum_pop_65p, ...)
lsoa$msoa <- sub("[A-Z]$", "", lsoa$name)
msoa <- aggregate(lsoa, by = "msoa", fun = "sum")

# Spread each MSOA total over its cells with the WorldPop pattern
ons <- transform_demand(
  x = msoa,
  value_col = "sum_pop",
  pmf = pattern,
  density = TRUE,
  full_output = TRUE  # also return the area totals
)

c(
  areas = nrow(msoa),
  ons_total = sum(msoa$sum_pop),
  grid_total = round(global(ons$surface, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]])
)

# Largest difference between an area's total and its grid total
largest_gap <- max(abs(ons$totals$original - ons$totals$redistributed))
signif(largest_gap, 2)
```

All `r nrow(msoa)` areas keep their totals: the largest difference is a tiny
fraction of a person. The new grid has the ONS counts with the WorldPop
pattern inside each area. The two sources differ in date and method, so their
ratio varies by area. The code summarizes the median ratio per area and maps
the ratio per cell, with the color scale capped at 0.5 and 1.5.

```{r ratio-map, fig.alt = sprintf("Raster map of mainland Cornwall showing, for each grid cell, the ONS mid-2024 count divided by the WorldPop 2020 count, on a blue-to-red scale capped at 0.5 and 1.5, with the %d MSOA boundaries in gray; each area has nearly one color, most areas are close to 1 or light red (ONS higher), a few are deep red and a few are blue (WorldPop higher).", nrow(msoa))}
# ONS count over WorldPop count in each cell, and its median per area
ratio <- crop(ons$surface / pop, msoa)
ratio_by_area <- extract(ratio, msoa, fun = median, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
round(summary(ratio_by_area), 2)

plot(
  clamp(ratio, 0.5, 1.5),
  axes = FALSE,
  range = c(0.5, 1.5),
  col = hcl.colors(50, "Blue-Red 3"),
  main = "ONS mid-2024 / WorldPop 2020 residents per cell"
)
lines(msoa, lwd = 0.3, col = "grey40")
```

Within an area both grids follow the WorldPop pattern, so each area has
nearly one color: the ratio of its two totals. In
`r sum(ratio_by_area > 1)` of the `r length(ratio_by_area)` areas the ONS
estimate is higher (the median ratio is `r round(median(ratio_by_area), 2)`),
and in one it is `r round(max(ratio_by_area), 1)` times the WorldPop count.
Choose the source that matches your question, say which you used, and keep to
it within one analysis. The other guides use the WorldPop grid directly.

If your raster is a density, people per square kilometer, multiply it by
`terra::cellSize(x, unit = "km")` first: longitude-latitude cells are not all
the same size.

### Spread a rate rather than a count

`rasterize_demand()` does a different job: it reweights a pattern by an area
**rate**, such as the share of residents aged 65 and over, and returns shares
of one total rather than counts that keep each area's total. The code builds
the older population on the grid this way and measures how much of each
area's known count it keeps.

```{r rate}
# Share of residents aged 65 and over in each MSOA
msoa$share_65 <- msoa$sum_pop_65p / msoa$sum_pop

# Reweight the WorldPop pattern by that share: the result is shares
older <- rasterize_demand(
  x = msoa,
  value_col = "share_65",
  prior = pattern
)
older_counts <- older * sum(msoa$sum_pop_65p)

# Each area's grid total as a fraction of its known count
kept <- extract(older_counts, msoa, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2] /
  msoa$sum_pop_65p
round(quantile(kept, c(0, 0.5, 1)), 2)
```

The shape is plausible: population times the local share aged 65 and over.
Area totals are not kept, though: the areas end up with between
`r round(min(kept), 2)` and `r round(max(kept), 2)` times their known count.
To place the older residents themselves, spread their counts:
`transform_demand(x = msoa, value_col = "sum_pop_65p", pmf = pattern, density = TRUE)`
keeps every area's total. Use `rasterize_demand()` when only the shape
matters, such as a relative weight per cell.

## Inputs for the allocation model

The allocation model, a conditional logit model (CLM, the standard model of a
choice among several options), gives each small area's residents a
probability of registering at each practice, or with the outside option: a
practice outside the data. It takes numeric inputs named by
ID: demand by small area, supply by practice and a matrix of travel minutes
between them, here `cornwall_travel`. The code prepares every small area and
practice, the Isles of Scilly included.

```{r allocation-na, error = TRUE}
# Every small area and practice, the Isles of Scilly included
all_areas <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_lsoa)
all_gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
all_demand <- setNames(all_areas$registered, all_areas$lsoa)
all_supply <- setNames(all_gp$gp_fte_extg, all_gp$practice)

prep_data(all_demand, all_supply, cornwall_travel)
```

Here an origin is a small area, where people live, and an active origin is
one with demand above zero. The error calls an area-practice pair an edge.
Unknown travel from an active origin is an error unless you say what it means. There are
three ways to say it. `missing_travel = "legacy_zero"` leaves
the unknown pairs out of the model, as the FCA indices do, and records that it
did. A travel time of `Inf` declares a pair known to have no link. That is a
known value, so `prep_data()` accepts it. Or you drop the rows and columns
with unknown times. The code shows the first two.

```{r allocation-policies}
# Leave the unknown pairs out, and record that policy
prep_data(all_demand, all_supply, cornwall_travel, missing_travel = "legacy_zero")

# Declare the unknown pairs known to have no link
no_link <- replace(cornwall_travel, is.na(cornwall_travel), Inf)
prep_data(all_demand, all_supply, no_link)
```

The first print records that every area has an unknown time (each mainland
area to the Scilly practice, and the Scilly area to the mainland practices)
and the policy that left them out. The second records none. In the allocation
model both give the pair no weight, so a model gives the same results with
either. They differ in what the data records: an unknown time for
`legacy_zero`, a known absence for `Inf`.

The guides drop the islands instead, as for the grid, with the small-area
recipe from [The Cornwall GP example
data](cornwall-data.html#small-areas-for-the-allocation-model). Its last line,
`obs_flows()`, comes in the next section:

```{r allocation-mainland}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
d
```

`prep_data()` lines up demand, supply and travel by their names, so their
order does not matter, and a supply name that matches no travel column stops
with an error. No area is left with an unknown travel time. The labels in
`metadata` stay with the data and with every result. spax does not convert
units.

## Observed counts in a long table

Observed counts usually arrive as a long table, one row per origin and
facility. `cornwall_flows` has one row per small area and practice with at
least one registration. `obs_flows()` says which column holds the origin IDs,
which the facility IDs and which the counts. A pair missing from the table
counts as 0, and duplicate pairs are added up.

```{r flows}
head(cornwall_flows)

flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
flows
```

`flows` declares all `r format(nrow(cornwall_flows), big.mark = ",")` rows,
the Isles of Scilly included. The print names the loss, Poisson by default,
which is how a fit compares modeled with observed counts. `spax()`
matches the rows to the IDs of the data when it fits a model, and says in a
message what it sets aside. The code fits the conditional logit model to the
mainland data.

```{r flows-message-numbers, include = FALSE}
scilly_area <- all_areas$lsoa[all_areas$scilly]
scilly_practice <- all_gp$practice[all_gp$scilly]
from_scilly_area <- sum(cornwall_flows$patients[cornwall_flows$lsoa == scilly_area])
mainland_at_scilly <- sum(cornwall_flows$patients[
  cornwall_flows$practice == scilly_practice & cornwall_flows$lsoa != scilly_area
])
```

```{r flows-fit}
clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
```

The `r format(from_scilly_area, big.mark = ",")` registrations of residents of
the Scilly small area are dropped, because that area is not in the data. The
`r mainland_at_scilly` registrations of mainland residents at the Scilly
practice are at a practice outside the data, so they belong to the outside
option. By default the fit does not know how many of an area's residents
registered outside the data, so it fits only the counts at the `r nrow(gp)`
practices, and these `r mainland_at_scilly` are left out. [Where do residents
register?](allocation-workflow.html) reads the fit and shows when the outside
counts can be declared known.

`spax()` matches the IDs of the observed counts to the data as text. If your
codes were read as numbers and lost their leading zeros, it matches each one
by its numeric value (1234 to `"01234"`) when exactly one ID of the data has
that value, and says so in a message. `prep_data()` makes no such allowance,
so keep IDs as text from the start.
